title: Inquest jury releases recommendations in death of man shot by police
subtitle: Police officers and firefighters need to undergo more training to respond to people experiencing mental health crises and they should hold debriefings after joint calls for service, according to a list of recommendations from an inquest jury.
article: Police officers and firefighters need to undergo more training to respond to people experiencing mental health crises and they should hold debriefings after joint calls for service, according to a list of recommendations from an inquest jury.

The jury released a list of nearly three-dozen recommendations following an inquest into the death of Wade Vander Wal, 44, who was shot dead by two OPP officers outside his family's Exeter house on Dec. 3, 2019, after emergency crews were called to a fire at the home.
Eleven witnesses testified during the eight-day inquest, a formal hearing where the facts of the death are laid out before a jury, which makes non-binding recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
The jury made 33 recommendations to the OPP, the South Huron Fire Department, the Ontario government and various ministries and government agencies.

Many of those recommendations seek to improve mental health training and funding, including creating a fourth-tier system for 911 calls to offer mental health as an option for the caller and providing incentives to recruit social workers and psychiatrists to rural communities.
At the opening day of the inquest , which ran from Sept. 18 to 27, inquest counsel Jar Dhar provided an overview of the anticipated evidence.
Emergency crews were called to Vander Wal's Exeter home after he was observed acting erratically and refused to leave his home when a neighbor spotted what appeared to be a small fire on the stove.

Vander Wal ignored demands from firefighters and police to leave the house before emerging with an axe after police used a battering ram to knock down the front door. One officer deployed a conducted-energy weapon (CEW), but it didn't stop Vander Wal's advance.

Officers fired several shots at Vander Wal, who fell to the ground with the axe still in his hands. An officer deployed a CEV, while another officer tried to get the axe away from Vander Wal. Another officer fired shots again. Vander Wal was taken to the Exeter hospital and pronounced dead. Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, cleared the officers involved of any wrongdoing .
Some of the jury's other recommendations aimed to improve policies, procedures and training for police, firefighters and emergency dispatchers.

For example, the jury recommended the OPP conduct a yearly review of "persons experiencing a mental health crisis checklist" to ensure officers are asking the appropriate questions. It also was recommended the OPP establish a process to ensure officers provide feedback to dispatchers when there's a lack of detailed or timely information at the scene.

Vander Wal's family didn't testify at the inquest, but his mother and sister both spoke at the opening day of the hearing, detailing the psychological fallout from his violent death and the difficult decision over whether to participate in the inquest.

"It will be worth it if there's a chance that changes can be made to prevent even one other person from losing their life in a mental health crisis or one other family having to go through this process," Vander Wal's sister, Sandy, said. "So, we ask you, the jury, what can you recommend (to prevent this) from this happening again and again? How do we ensure that this is just not words and wishes?"
